themes.label: Motivation for range-based stochastic volatility estimation
themes.need: Someone choosing an estimation method for a stochastic volatility model needs the motivation for range-based Gaussian QML - the inefficiency of return-based QML, the practical difficulties of GMM/likelihood-based alternatives, and a preview of the paper's efficiency, normality, and microstructure-robustness results for the range.

themes.label: Continuous-time SV model and its discretization
themes.need: Someone specifying a stochastic volatility model needs the continuous-time diffusion formulation (price and log-volatility as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) and its discrete-time approximation, including the resulting AR(1) dynamics for log volatility.

themes.label: State-space representation and QML estimation
themes.need: Someone wanting to estimate a discretized stochastic volatility model from an observable volatility proxy needs the homogeneity property that turns any proxy into a noisy signal of log volatility, the resulting linear state-space (transition/measurement) representation, and the Gaussian quasi-maximum-likelihood estimation approach via the Kalman filter, including its known consistency-but-inefficiency tradeoff.

themes.label: Distributional properties: return-based vs. range-based proxies
themes.need: Someone choosing a volatility proxy for QML estimation needs the theoretical distribution (mean, skewness, kurtosis) of log absolute/squared returns versus log range for a driftless Brownian motion, showing the log range is both far more efficient and far closer to Gaussian than return-based proxies.
themes.distributed_justification: b007-b008 form one continuous comparison of return-based and range-based proxy distributions; the gap at 184-186 is Pass-A trash (Table I caption), not a thematic break.

themes.label: Robustness of the range to microstructure noise (theory)
themes.need: Someone worried that microstructure noise (bid-ask bounce) contaminates a high-frequency volatility proxy needs the theoretical argument and simulated illustration that realized volatility is severely biased upward by bid-ask bounce while the range is only mildly affected, because the range's extremes partially cancel the bounce-induced bias.
themes.distributed_justification: b009-b010 form one continuous argument for range robustness (theoretical mechanism plus its simulated illustration); the gap at 232-234 is Pass-A trash (Figure 2 caption), not a thematic break.

themes.label: Monte Carlo comparison of QML range vs. QML/exact-ML absolute return
themes.need: Someone wanting quantitative evidence that range-based QML dominates absolute-return-based QML and even exact ML needs the Monte Carlo simulation design (Euler discretization, eq. 16), the resulting bias/RMSE comparison of the three estimators for rho, beta, and mean log volatility (Tables II-III at T=1000 and T=500), and the interpretation isolating how much of the gain comes from normality alone versus the extra intraday information in the range.

themes.label: Small-N range bias and Kalman-filter volatility extraction
themes.need: Someone using range-based QML with infrequent intraday sampling needs the small-sample-size (few-trades-per-day) bias pattern of the range estimator, and the Kalman-filter volatility-extraction results showing range-based extractions remain more accurate than return-based ones even accounting for this bias.

themes.label: Range vs. realized volatility under microstructure noise (Monte Carlo)
themes.need: Someone deciding between range-based and realized-volatility estimators for noisy high-frequency data needs the systematic Monte Carlo comparison (Table IV) showing realized volatility dominates under true prices but the range dominates once bid-ask bounce contaminates observed prices, and how this relative advantage changes with sampling interval.
themes.distributed_justification: b018-b020 form one continuous microstructure-robustness simulation narrative; the gap at 492-499 is Pass-A trash (Figure 4/5 captions), not a thematic break.

themes.label: Exchange-rate data and construction of volatility proxies
themes.need: Someone wanting to replicate the exchange-rate volatility-dynamics application needs the choice of five U.S. dollar exchange rates, the use of daily high/low/close currency-futures prices (vs. spot) and the justification for that choice, and the data period/construction details.

themes.label: One-factor SV model estimates and their misspecification
themes.need: Someone fitting a one-factor stochastic volatility model to exchange-rate data needs Table V's proxy distribution/autocorrelation statistics, Table VI's one-factor QML parameter estimates for five currencies, and the residual-diagnostic evidence that the one-factor model is misspecified.

themes.label: Two-factor SV model and its adequacy
themes.need: Someone extending to a two-factor stochastic volatility specification needs the two-factor transition equation (eq. 17-20), Table VI's two-factor estimates and Table VIII's residual diagnostics showing the two-factor model is adequate (serially uncorrelated residuals), and the empirical confirmation that the log-range measurement-equation residuals are indeed close to Gaussian.

themes.label: Why two factors: range's informational advantage and long-memory link
themes.need: Someone wanting the intuition for why range-based analysis reveals two volatility factors while return-based analysis does not needs the explanation that the range's low measurement error lets estimation target both the autocorrelation and the volatility-of-volatility of the true process, and the discussion connecting this two-factor structure to fractionally-integrated long-memory volatility as an alternative reduced-form description.
